issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, this appraisal is a poor thematic fit because it implies an interpersonal perpetrator threat ('who will harm you') rather than danger from impersonal environmental forces. The rest of the profile is built around disaster-related ongoing danger/hypervigilance and intrusive reliving, so this item stands out as clinically incongruent with the specified trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe classic fear-based re-experiencing and hypervigilance, but there is no accompanying content suggesting perpetration, moral injury, or a specific action during the disaster that would plausibly drive a strong violated-values appraisal.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' could occur after a disaster, but here it sits awkwardly with the otherwise generic fear/reliving profile. There are no memory or threat items about failing to protect family, losing dependents, or role-related guilt, so this item lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'I need to stay alert' while trying to sleep is more characteristic of an ongoing human threat context than of a completed natural disaster, especially when paired with scanning exits and staying near exits in all buildings. Taken together, these threat items imply anticipation of intentional attack or entrapment rather than the specific threat structure suggested by the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is not impossible, but it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile for a 65-year-old married male retail worker with natural-disaster trauma. The rest of the profile centers on ongoing danger, hypervigilance, and intrusive reliving; this item instead implies a specific role-based self-evaluation that is not supported by the other selected appraisals, memory, threat, or coping items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'Other-Blame Rumination' sits awkwardly with a natural-disaster trauma profile. Blame can occur, but this item specifically focuses on dwelling on what other people have done to me, whereas the rest of the profile describes threat and reliving linked to impersonal environmental danger rather than interpersonal harm or betrayal. Without any corroborating appraisal or memory content involving preventable human actions, this item is clinically hard to reconcile.

vignette:
Kwame is a 65-year-old married man who has spent years working on the floor of a large retail store, where he helps customers, restocks shelves, and spends long shifts under bright lights and near the automatic front doors. He traces the change in himself to a hurricane that tore through his neighborhood two years ago. During the storm, the power failed in the middle of the night and the house seemed to shake around him. He and his wife moved from room to room listening to windows rattle and objects strike the siding, trying to judge whether they would need to get out. What stayed with him most was the feeling of being trapped while the danger closed in from all sides, scanning in the dark for the quickest way out if the roof gave way. Even after the storm passed, he had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that surviving had not left him relieved so much as altered; in his mind, he had permanently changed for the worse, into someone who could never again afford to let his guard down.

That belief hardened over the following months. Kwame was certain he now had to be on guard all the time, and this conviction shaped how he moved through ordinary life. The same conviction made the hurricane easier to fall back into: each time he told himself that the world was dangerous and that he had been permanently changed, his mind returned to the dark house and the shaking walls as if the memory were confirming what he already feared about himself and the world. At work, the first thing he did on entering the break room, stockroom, or sales floor was locate the nearest exit. He positioned himself so he could stay close to a door, and while talking with customers he found his eyes moving past their faces to doorways, corners, and signs of possible danger. He distracted himself by fussing with tasks, straightening displays repeatedly or focusing on small bits of restocking, because if his mind went quiet the storm came back too vividly. In his own understanding, these habits were necessary; if the world was dangerous and he was no longer the man he used to be, staying near an exit and constantly checking his surroundings felt like the only sensible way to get through the day.

His memories of the hurricane are not like a story he can tell from start to finish. He describes them as a film that plays over and over: the shriek of wind, the darkness after the power cut, the sense that the walls might split. When it comes back, he does not feel that he is remembering something finished. He feels as if it is happening right now. In those moments the event seems present rather than past, and that immediacy drives home his belief that danger is everywhere and that something in him has been permanently damaged. The memory itself becomes proof, to him, that he has not truly come through it.

Because the memories arrive with that force, his body and attention stay keyed up. At night he has difficulty falling asleep because he feels he needs to remain alert, as though sleep would leave him unprepared for the next disaster. Entering any room, even a familiar one, he scans for exits almost automatically. He is superalert, watchful, on guard. The reverse is true as well: the more vigilant he becomes, the more likely he is to catch some small cue—a hard rain against the store windows, a sudden dimming of lights, the slam of a loading-bay door—and the film starts again. On the sales floor during thunderstorms, he can feel himself pulled out of the present and back into that night, his chest tight, his mind insisting that what happened before could happen again at any moment.

This constant sense of threat has steadily narrowed his life. Staying close to exits and checking the environment give him a brief feeling of control, but they also keep confirming his view that danger is always near. When he sees himself unable to stand in the middle of a room without plotting an escape route, it seems to him further evidence that he has changed for the worse. The same pattern plays out at work: because he is scanning so intently, he rarely feels settled with customers, and he often shifts his position to keep a clear path to the door. He distracts himself to get through his shift, yet the effort of doing that leaves him exhausted and no less watchful. Each precaution tells him the danger must be real; each night of lying awake on alert convinces him again that the world is unsafe.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was worn down by the sense that the hurricane had never really ended inside him. His wife had begun to notice that even at home he was always checking where the exits were and rarely relaxed enough to fall asleep easily. He came to treatment because he was frightened by how present the storm still felt and by what that seemed to say about him. More than anything, he fears that this guarded, altered version of himself is permanent, but he is also hoping, cautiously, that he might learn how to live in a room without first preparing to escape it.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly state in any single paragraph that Kwame’s negative beliefs or appraisals directly lead to or intensify the trauma memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
